newsitem.title: USA: Feds must assume some DC costs - House panel chair.
newsitem.headline: Feds must assume some DC costs - House panel chair.

text.p: The chairman of a key U.S. House panel on Monday said the federal government must take over some of the financial responsibilities of the ailing District of Columbia.

Rep. Thomas Davis, R-Va., chairman of the House Government Reform Committee's subpanel on D.C., said in an interview with CNN, "We're going to have to move around some of the responsibilities that the capital city has to provide for itself. And there may be some increase of federal presence or help."
Asked whether that means the federal government will assume some costs, Davis said, "Right."
"For example, there's an unfunded pension liability that the city assumed. And, frankly, Congress got a good deal (in) giving it to the city," Davis said.
"(But) the city can't afford to do all of that. We're going to have some increased liability there," Davis said.
Davis also said D.C. "is really not capable" of funding operation of maximum security prisons, one of its current jobs.
"It's a big problem. It's far greater than the city can cope with. We're going to need some federal help in that area," Davis said.
Asked whether Congress is contemplating a federal takeover of the city, Davis said, "No." He said D.C.'s current structure as a kind of city-state with aid from the federal government is viable.

"And even if it is not viable, changing it would be very, very tough at this point. Congress is not going to give the city statehood. And I don't think the American people will. Maryland doesn't want its section back. So it's a tough problem," Davis said.
Up until recently, Davis has said Congress will not give D.C. more dollars until city officials slash spending further.
But, on December 13, President Clinton said that D.C.'s problems are due, in part, to its confusing status as part city, part state. He pledged a "systematic effort" to address the problem.
Clinton was responding to a hard-hitting "strategic plan" issued on December 12 by D.C.'s control board.
The panel warned that D.C. will never emerge from financial crisis unless the U.S. government steps up to the plate and agrees to finance up to $1 billion in city programs.
They include Medicaid, mental health care, prisons and infrastructure. The federal government also must take over some of the city's massive pension liability, the board said.
In other parts of the country, such services are routinely financed by states.
The control board report sets out a detailed timetable for tackling the city' problems.
By March 31, for instance, the board will recommend key structural changes in city financing, including more detailed proposals on what costs should be assumed by the federal government.
